invasive-species-s1.title: Mussels in a lake after an invader arrived

table.caption: Mussels per square meter of lake bottom in the years after an invasive mussel arrived (invented data for practice)

invasive-species-s2.title: An invasive and a native mussel over ten years

options: It is nonnative, spreads fast and causes harm
It is any species that was introduced by people
It is a native species whose population is falling
It is a species that lives in more than one biome

why.correct: Nonnative is not the same as invasive: a species is invasive when it spreads beyond control and causes harm.
options: Right: invasive species are introduced, spread rapidly and harm ecosystems, economies or health.
Many introduced species never spread or cause harm; only some become invasive.
A falling native population is a sign of decline, not invasion.
Living in several biomes does not make a species invasive.

items.q: Which traits help a nonnative species become invasive?
options: A narrow diet and slow reproduction
A broad diet and fast reproduction
A need for one kind of habitat and few offspring
Large body size and a long time to maturity

why.correct: Invasive species are usually generalists with r-selected traits: they tolerate many conditions and reproduce quickly.
options: Those are specialist, K-selected traits, which make spreading hard.
Right: generalists find food almost anywhere, and many offspring let numbers explode.
A narrow habitat need and few young limit spread.
Slow maturity limits how fast a population can grow.

items.q: A student writes that an invasive species succeeds because of its trait "no predators." Why would an exam reader not accept this as a trait?
options: Invasive species usually have many predators in their new home
Predators have no effect on how a species spreads
Lacking predators describes its new habitat, not the species
The answer should name a predator that eats it

why.correct: Name a trait of the organism (generalist diet, high reproductive rate, tolerance of many conditions); "no natural predators" describes the new ecosystem.
options: Invasive species often meet few predators; that is about the setting, not a trait.
Few predators do help spread; the issue is that it is not a trait.
Right: a trait belongs to the organism, such as fast reproduction or a broad diet.
The question asks for a trait of the species itself.

items.q: Describe how the invasive mussel population changed over the 10 years.
options: Steady, even growth each year
Fast growth, then a crash to zero
A steady decline from year 0 to year 10
Slow, then explosive, then level

why.correct: The invader’s curve is S-shaped: slow start, rapid growth, then leveling off as it nears its carrying capacity.
options: Growth was very uneven: small at first, then huge.
The population leveled off; it did not crash.
The invader rose; the native mussel declined.
Right: under 30 per m² for 3 years, a jump to 1,200 by year 7, then near 1,400.

items.q: By what percent did the native mussel population change from year 0 to year 10?

mistakes.why: You divided by the new value. Use (new − old) ÷ old × 100: (2 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100.
The size is right, but the population fell, so the change is negative: −95%.

items.q: The lake bottom covers 3,000 m². Write the setup for the total number of invasive mussels in year 10, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Density times area gives the total. Multiply 1,420 per m² by 3,000 m².
In year 10 the density is 1,420 per m², not 1,400 (that is year 9).
1,420 is the number per square meter. Multiply by the 3,000 m² of lake bottom: 4,260,000 mussels.

items.q: Which explanation best fits the decline of the native mussel?
options: The native mussel died of old age
The lake became too cold for mussels
The invader outcompeted it for food and space
The native mussel moved to a new lake

why.correct: An invader crowding out a native for the same resources is interspecific competition; invasive mussels also attach directly to native mussels’ shells.
options: A whole population does not die of old age in a few years.
The invader thrived, so the lake still suited mussels.
Right: the native fell as the invader rose, the pattern of competition.
Mussels attached to the bottom do not migrate between lakes.

items.q: In the figure, in which year did the invasive mussel first pass 1,000 per m²?
options: Year 5
Year 9
Year 3
Year 7

why.correct: Read the left axis: the invader crosses 1,000 between year 6 (800) and year 7 (1,200).
options: In year 5 it was 350 per m².
It passed 1,000 two years earlier, in year 7.
In year 3 it was only 30 per m².
Right: it was 800 in year 6 and 1,200 in year 7.

items.q: Why does the figure use two vertical axes?
options: The two populations differ greatly in size
The two species live in different lakes
Time runs differently for each species
The native is counted per lake, the invader per m²

why.correct: A second axis lets two very different scales be compared on one graph; always check which axis a line uses.
options: Right: on one axis, the native’s 40 per m² would look flat next to 1,400.
Both are in the same lake.
Both share the same time axis.
Both are per square meter.

items.q: When would control of the invader have been cheapest and most likely to work?
options: In year 10, after the native was gone
In years 0 to 3, when it was still rare
In year 7, at its fastest growth
At any time, since the cost is the same

why.correct: Prevention and early detection are far cheaper than control once an invader is established.
options: By then the invader is everywhere and the native is nearly lost.
Right: early detection and rapid response stop an invader before it explodes.
By year 7 there were over 1,000 per m².
Control gets far harder and costlier as an invader spreads.

items.q: Zebra mussels from Europe arrived in the Great Lakes in the late 1980s. How did they most likely get there?
options: By swimming across the Atlantic Ocean
On the feet of migrating birds from Europe
In ballast water released by cargo ships
Released as pets by aquarium owners

why.correct: Ballast water is a major pathway; rules now require ships to exchange or treat it before entering the Great Lakes.
options: Zebra mussels cannot cross an ocean on their own.
This is not how they reached the Great Lakes.
Right: ships took on water in Europe and released it, with mussel larvae, in the Great Lakes.
Ballast water, not the pet trade, is the accepted route.

items.q: Kudzu was planted in the southern United States to control soil erosion. What unintended effect followed?
options: It increased soil erosion across the South
It died out in the first cold winter
It became rare across the South
It smothered trees and native plants

why.correct: A solution to one problem can create another: erosion control led to a vine that blankets forests.
options: Kudzu holds soil; the problem is that it smothers other plants.
Kudzu survives and spreads across much of the South.
Kudzu is invasive and widespread, not at risk of dying out.
Right: kudzu grows fast and smothers whatever it covers.

items.q: Cane toads were brought to Australia to eat beetles in sugar cane fields. Instead, they spread across northern Australia. Which lesson does this best show?
options: A control species can itself become invasive
Biological control works better than chemicals in each case
Toads are specialists that eat just one kind of beetle
Native predators quickly learned to eat cane toads

why.correct: Introducing a species to control another must be tested carefully; a generalist can become the bigger problem.
options: Right: cane toads ate little of the beetle and spread, poisoning native predators.
This case shows biological control can fail badly.
Cane toads are generalists, which helped them spread.
Many native predators die after eating the toxic toads.

items.q: Which actions help prevent or control invasive species? Select all that apply.
options: Requiring ships to treat ballast water
Cleaning boats before moving them between lakes
Releasing unwanted aquarium fish into local streams
Planting fast-growing nonnative vines for erosion control

why.correct: Prevention (inspection, cleaning, ballast rules) works best; early detection and removal come next.
options: Right: it kills larvae before they are released.
Right: it removes mussels and plants hitching a ride.
That is how some invaders get started.
That is how kudzu spread.

items.q: Propose a solution, other than using chemicals, to stop zebra mussels from spreading to a new lake used by boaters.

why.correct: Respect "other than": a non-chemical prevention step fitted to how the invader travels.

action.label: Solution
options: boats to be cleaned and drained at the boat ramp
more chemical treatment of the lake
more fishing boats on the lake

why.1: The question says other than chemicals.
why.2: More boats would spread mussels faster.

how.label: How it works
options: mussels and larvae are removed before boats enter
mussels grow faster
native mussels move away

why.1: The goal is to stop mussels, not help them.
why.2: Moving native mussels is not the aim.

effect.label: Effect
options: prevents the invader from reaching the new lake
adds nutrients to the lake
raises the water level

why.1: Cleaning boats does not add nutrients.
why.2: Cleaning boats does not change water level.

specific.model: Require boats to be cleaned, drained and dried at the boat ramp so that mussels and larvae are removed before boats enter the lake, which prevents the invader from reaching the new lake because boats are how it moves between lakes.
